results.result: Four 3D-EM datasets were acquired from mouse cortical regions (S1, V2, PPC, ACC) at the L1/2 border using SBEM with voxel sizes of 11.24-12 × 11.24-12 × 28-30 nm³, following approved ethical protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C64, C65 provide detailed methodological specifications for data acquisition that are internally consistent and appropriately documented. Claims C72-C74 confirm ethical compliance. The technical specifications are standard for SBEM and the anatomical targeting is clearly justified.

results.result: L2 pyramidal cells receive significantly higher shaft synapse density (0.42±0.02 vs 0.22±0.02 synapses/µm) and shaft synapse fraction (33.6±17.9% vs 9.9±5.1%) at their main bifurcations compared to deeper layer (L3/5) pyramidal cells, representing a ~3-fold difference.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C9 provide quantitative measurements with appropriate statistical testing (p<10⁻¹¹) from a substantial dataset (6240 total synapses on 82 ADs, C61-C63). The measurements include both density and fractional metrics, with consistent findings across multiple cortical regions (C1). Statistical parameters (mean±SEM/SD, sample sizes) are properly reported.

results.result: Axons show nearly binary targeting preference for either dendritic shafts or spines: 91/92 shaft-seeded axons made ≥80% of synapses onto shafts, and 34/35 spine-seeded axons made ≥80% onto spines, enabling classification of shaft-preferring axons as putative inhibitory and spine-preferring as excitatory with >75% accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 provide strong quantitative evidence for axonal targeting specificity with clear numerical support. The bimodal distribution (Figure 2b) and high prediction accuracy (>90% for most cell types, C14) validate the classification scheme. This is further supported by citation to Motta et al., 2019 (C13).

results.result: Synapse size onto spines was similar between L2 and DL ADs, but shaft synapses were slightly larger on L2 ADs. Multiple spine innervations were rare (6.4±0.9% for L2, 3.5±0.4% for DL ADs).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 provide comparative measurements with statistical testing. The findings indicate that synapse size differences would enhance rather than counteract the observed inhibitory density differences. Low rates of multiple spine innervations (C17) confirm that this phenomenon does not confound the main results.

results.result: L2 ADs are 21% wider than DL ADs at their main bifurcation (2.16±0.06 µm vs 1.77±0.04 µm), yet still receive 59% higher putative inhibitory synapse density per unit surface area.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 address a potential confound (dendritic diameter) and demonstrate that the inhibitory density difference persists even when normalized to surface area. The measurements include appropriate statistical testing (p<10⁻⁴) and sample size (n=82). This strengthens the main finding by ruling out a geometric explanation.

results.result: Inhibitory axons show strong cell-type-specific targeting: axons seeded from DL ADs preferentially reinnervate DL ADs (71.2±3% of AD synapses) over L2 ADs (28.8%), while L2-seeded axons preferentially target L2 ADs (77.4% of AD synapses), despite similar axonal path lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 demonstrate connectomic specificity with strong statistical support (p<10⁻⁸, C23-C24). The finding that axonal path lengths are indistinguishable (C27) rules out simple spatial proximity as an explanation, indicating genuine cell-type-specific targeting. Sample size is substantial (n=183 axons).

results.result: Inhibitory axons predominantly form monosynaptic connections with ADs (77% single synapse), with similar synapse numbers per target for L2-seeded (1.32±0.05) and DL-seeded (1.29±0.04) axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide quantitative characterization of connection multiplicity with appropriate statistical testing (p=0.83, showing no significant difference between groups). This finding indicates that the observed targeting specificity is not driven by multiple innervations of the same target.

results.result: Axonal targeting preferences show remarkable consistency across cortical regions (S1, V2, PPC, ACC), with coefficients of variation ranging from 19.2% to 69.1% for different target types.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 provide quantitative measures of cross-regional consistency. The relatively low CVs for most measurements indicate that the observed connectivity patterns are general principles rather than region-specific phenomena. This is further supported by Figure 4 showing statistical comparisons across regions.

results.result: L5 thick-tufted (L5tt) and slender-tufted (L5st) pyramidal cells were distinguished by hierarchical clustering of morphological features, with L5tt showing significantly higher spine density (1.4±0.24 vs 0.59±0.13 spines/µm, p=0.004).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 describe a valid cell-type classification approach using multiple morphological features (soma diameter, AD diameter, oblique dendrites, bifurcation depth). The resulting spine density difference (C33) validates the classification. Statistical testing is appropriate (Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

results.result: At the main bifurcation, L2 pyramidal cells show uniquely high putative inhibitory synapse fraction (38.0±4.9%), significantly higher than L3 (7.8±0.8%), L5tt (8.7±1.1%), and L5st (15.3±3.0%) cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 provide comprehensive cell-type-specific measurements with appropriate statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis test p<10⁻⁴, post-hoc Tukey's test). The finding that L2 cells are unique (C40) is well-supported by the quantitative data showing clear separation from other cell types. Sample size is adequate (n=40).

results.result: In L5 pyramidal cells, putative inhibitory synapse fraction is strongly anti-correlated with thick-tuftedness (PC1), primarily driven by increased excitatory synapse density in L5tt neurons (R²=0.74, p<10⁻⁵).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 provide correlation analysis with strong statistical support. The mechanistic interpretation (C42) that excitatory density drives the effect is supported by the high R² value and is consistent with the data in Figure 5f. The analysis appropriately uses principal component analysis to quantify thick-tuftedness.

results.result: Two identified L2 marginal neurons (L2MN) showed putative inhibitory synapse fractions (53.2% and 27.8%) consistent with other L2 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 reports measurements from only two neurons, which is insufficient for statistical conclusions about this cell subtype. While the values fall within the range of other L2 neurons, the small sample size prevents definitive conclusions about whether L2MN constitute a distinct subtype or share properties with regular L2 neurons.

results.result: Putative inhibitory synapse fraction at the main bifurcation shows strong distance-dependence on soma distance (R²=0.73), which is stronger than the distance-dependence of absolute synapse densities (R²=0.01 for excitatory, 0.56 for inhibitory).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 provide correlation analysis with strong goodness-of-fit measures. The finding that the ratio shows stronger distance-dependence than absolute densities (C45) is interesting and well-supported by the R² values. Sample size is substantial (n=81). This suggests a distance-dependent mechanism regulating the balance of excitation and inhibition.

results.result: L5 pyramidal cells show increased putative inhibitory input at distal dendrites: L5tt cells show 3-fold decrease in excitatory density with stable inhibitory density (22.5±1.7% inhibitory fraction distally), while L5st cells show 31.3±1.8% inhibitory fraction at distal tufts.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 provide quantitative measurements of spatial gradients with appropriate statistical testing (p<10⁻³ for L5tt, p=0.005 for L5st). The findings are based on substantial data (n=4506 synapses on 14 dendrites). The results demonstrate cell-type-specific spatial organization of inhibitory input.

results.result: L2 pyramidal cells show opposite spatial gradient to L5 cells: putative inhibitory density decreases ~2-fold toward distal tufts while excitatory input increases ~1.5-fold, yielding ~3-fold reduction in inhibitory fraction (34.6±2.5% at main bifurcation vs 11.4±1.4% at distal tufts).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide quantitative measurements with strong statistical support (p<10⁻⁴). The finding of opposite spatial gradients in L2 vs L5 cells is a key result demonstrating cell-type-specific organization. Sample size is substantial (n=62 dendritic segments).

results.result: L3 pyramidal cells show homogeneous inhibitory input fraction along their apical dendrites: 7.8±0.8% at main bifurcation and 10.2±0.9% at distal tufts, with no significant spatial dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 demonstrate lack of spatial gradient in L3 cells through appropriate statistical testing showing no significant differences (p=0.36 vs L5tt at main bifurcation, p=0.84 vs L2 at distal tufts). This finding distinguishes L3 cells from both L2 and L5 cells, supporting the conclusion that each cell type has a unique inhibitory profile.

results.result: Each pyramidal cell type (L2, L3, L5tt, L5st) shows distinct putative inhibitory innervation profiles along apical dendrites, with cell-type-specific inhibitory-to-excitatory ratios and axonal targeting preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58, C77 synthesize the major findings into a coherent conclusion. The distinct profiles are well-supported by the quantitative data from multiple preceding results. The claim of cell-type specificity (C77) is justified by the comprehensive characterization across multiple cell types and dendritic locations. This represents the primary conclusion of the manuscript.

results.result: Synapses were identified based on vesicle cloud and postsynaptic density presence, without considering symmetry of pre- and postsynaptic densities.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 describes the synapse identification method. While this approach differs from traditional Gray's Type I/II classification, it is justified by the subsequent validation through axonal targeting analysis (C10-C14). The method is appropriate for SBEM data where in-plane resolution may be limited.

results.result: The study targets the L1/2 border where 80-90% of cortical pyramidal cells form their main bifurcation, a site implicated in controlling regenerative electrical events and receiving long-range inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C59, C60 provide anatomical and functional context supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. Claims C67-C68 cite relevant physiological findings about GABA-B receptors and hippocampal inhibitory gradients. These claims establish the biological significance of the study region.

results.result: L5 pyramidal cells in cortex exhibit a distal inhibitory domain similar to hippocampal pyramidal cells, but this domain is absent in L2 and L3 pyramidal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 compare the current findings to prior work in hippocampus (C68). The comparison is valid and supported by the data showing increased distal inhibitory fraction in L5 cells (C47-C48) but not in L2 (C49-C50) or L3 cells (C51-C53). This highlights both conservation and divergence of circuit organization principles.

results.result: Previous light microscopy work using Gephyrin tagging underestimated spine rates by ~20% compared to complete 3D EM sampling, leading to overestimation of inhibitory-to-excitatory ratios for L3 pyramidal cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 provides methodological comparison to prior work (Iascone et al., 2018) with appropriate citations. The critique is valid as complete 3D EM reconstruction would be expected to detect more spines than light microscopy-based methods. This highlights the advantage of the current approach.

results.result: The findings describe connectomic principles for pyramidal cell control at apical dendrites and support differential computational properties of L2, L3, and L5 pyramidal cell subtypes, suggesting differential modes of inhibitory operation.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76, C81-C82 represent the main conclusions and implications of the work. These are well-supported by the comprehensive quantitative characterization of cell-type-specific inhibitory innervation patterns (multiple preceding results). The inference of differential computational properties is reasonable given the distinct synaptic input compositions, though direct functional validation would strengthen this claim.

results.result: L5tt pyramidal cells may be controlled by overall and slow inhibition at main bifurcations (via non-synaptic GABA-B receptors) but specific synaptic innervation at distal dendrites, while L2 pyramidal cells receive specific synaptic inhibition at main bifurcations.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 propose mechanistic interpretations combining the current anatomical findings with prior physiological data (C67). While the integration is logical, the claims are speculative (indicated by "may indicate" in the source text). The low synaptic inhibitory innervation at L5tt main bifurcations is consistent with non-synaptic GABA-B control, but direct functional evidence is lacking.

results.result: The distinct putative inhibitory input profile of L3 pyramidal cells may suggest they allow for specific computations not shared by L2 or L5 pyramidal cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is explicitly speculative ("may suggest") about computational implications. While the anatomical distinctiveness of L3 cells is well-established (C51-C53), the functional/computational consequences require experimental validation. The claim is reasonable but remains a hypothesis.
